newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian government expected to win confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Italian government expected to win confidence vote.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi was widely expected to win a parliamentary vote of confidence later on Wednesday which he has called to ram into law a salvage plan for the ailing southern bank, Banco di Napoli.
However government proposals to reform Italy's leaking fiscal system faced much stiffer opposition both from inside and outside Prodi's centre-left administration.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi announced the confidence debate in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) on Tuesday after the separatist Northern League party threatened to scupper a decree covering debt-laden Banco di Napoli.
Victory in the vote, set for around 1830 GMT, would ensure the legislation becomes law while defeat would bring Prodi down.
His six-month old coalition does not control the lower house of parliament and depends for its majority on the hard left Communist Refoundation party.

The opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance, which draws much of its support from the poorer south, is not expected to cause trouble over Banco di Napoli, which is seen as an important investment machine for southern Italy.
"Although we do not entirely support government plans for Banco di Napoli...we nonetheless support the decree," said a spokesman for the centrist CCD-CDU group -- a member of the Freedom Alliance.
The Treasury wants to inject two trillion lire ($1.3 billion) of state funds into the heavily indebted bank and privatise it before the end of the year.
The League, who have become masters at parliamentary filibustering, have presented 1,001 amendments to the decree and demanded similar state subsidies for the north.
But if objections to the Banco di Napoli decree looked set to be brushed aside, widespread dissent over plans for a radical shake-up of Italy's tax system seemed harder to sort out.

The finance ministry, looking to combat rampant fiscal fraud, wants to introduce a new regional tax, aimed at companies, and revise personal taxation. In addition the government plans to raise some 13 trillion lire next year from a once-off "Euro Tax", which has yet to be specified.

The Freedom Alliance, headed by former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, has blasted the proposals as an attack on the middle classes while small businesses have said they will stage protests "to the limits of the law" against the fiscal plans.
Prodi issued a severe statement on Tuesday saying he would not tolerate any illegal actions but he has still to convince his parliamentary allies to back the revision.
Two meetings of government parliamentary party leaders on Tuesday failed to come up with an agreement and another meeting was planned for later on Wednesday.

The Communist Refoundation wants the government to drop the personal taxation changes, while the Italian Renewal party, headed by Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, wants both these and the new regional tax to be scrapped.
